name: Radiomics
title: Radiomics
answer: Radiomics is the high-throughput extraction of quantitative features from standard medical images such as CT, MRI, and PET scans. It turns regions of interest into mineable data that describe shape, texture, intensity, and spatial relationships within a tumor or organ. These features are intended to reveal patterns that are not visible to the naked eye and to support diagnosis, prognosis, or treatment response assessment. Radiomics sits between routine image interpretation and machine learning, feeding structured image data into statistical and predictive models.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Radiomics is the high-throughput extraction of quantitative features from standard medical images such as CT, MRI, and PET scans. It turns regions of interest into mineable data that describe shape, texture, intensity, and spatial relationships within a tumor or organ. These features are intended to reveal patterns that are not visible to the naked eye and to support diagnosis, prognosis, or treatment response assessment. Radiomics sits between routine image interpretation and machine learning, feeding structured image data into statistical and predictive models.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Radiomics workflows run on existing imaging archives and picture archiving and communication systems, with additional software for segmentation and feature computation. The work typically requires access to DICOM images, consistent acquisition protocols, and computing resources for batch processing of large cohorts. Feature extraction can be performed with open source libraries or commercial research platforms, but the underlying infrastructure is usually a hospital or research imaging database rather than a dedicated hardware device. Data storage and version control matter because feature sets must be linked back to the original scans and clinical records.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done in a sequence of image acquisition, region of interest segmentation, feature extraction, feature selection, and model building. A radiologist or trained annotator first outlines the tumor or organ, then software computes hundreds or thousands of numerical features from that region. These features are filtered for stability and redundancy before being used to train a classifier or regression model against a clinical endpoint. The method depends heavily on reproducible segmentation and on testing whether features remain stable across different scanners, reconstruction settings, and observers.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in radiomics center on data provenance, patient privacy, and the reproducibility of published feature sets. Models can inherit bias from imaging protocols, patient populations, or annotation practices, and a feature that works in one hospital may fail in another because of scanner or reconstruction differences. Regulatory oversight is still maturing, and radiomic models used for clinical decisions may require validation as medical devices or decision support tools. Clear documentation of image sources, preprocessing steps, and segmentation rules is necessary for any claim of clinical utility.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Radiomics is moving toward tighter integration with deep learning, where neural networks learn features directly from images and may be combined with handcrafted radiomic features. The field is also shifting from single-institution retrospective studies to prospective, multicenter validation and harmonization of imaging data. Future work is likely to focus on linking radiomic signatures with genomics, pathology, and longitudinal outcomes, and on making feature extraction robust enough for routine clinical reporting rather than research-only use.
